group.title: Rare nouns
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A paid job that needs almost no work.
examples: His post on the board was a {sinecure}; he attended one meeting a year.
wrong: The sinecure kept her working fourteen hours a day.

words.meaning: A small but real amount of something good.
examples: With a {modicum} of luck, we’ll finish by Friday.
wrong: He showed a modicum of patience by waiting three whole years.

words.meaning: A small, basic amount of knowledge or a few scattered things.
examples: She has a {smattering} of Italian, enough to order food.
wrong: With his smattering of French, he translated the whole novel perfectly.

words.meaning: A confused mixture of different things, often nonsense.
examples: The report was a {farrago} of rumors and half-truths.
wrong: The farrago of facts was clear, neat and well ordered.

words.meaning: Something with layers of older marks or history still visible under newer ones.
examples: The old city is a {palimpsest} of Roman, medieval and modern streets.
wrong: The palimpsest was a fresh page with nothing ever written on it.

words.meaning: A large, rich supply of many different things.
examples: The market was a {cornucopia} of fruit, spices and cheese.
wrong: The empty shelves were a cornucopia of nothing at all.

words.meaning: The lowest or worst point of something.
examples: The team reached its {nadir} with ten losses in a row.
wrong: Winning the title was the nadir of her brilliant career.

words.meaning: The highest point of success or power.
examples: The empire reached its {apogee} in the second century.
wrong: At its apogee, the company was close to closing down.

words.meaning: A sign or person that shows something is coming soon.
examples: The first swallows are a {harbinger} of spring.
wrong: The harbinger arrived long after the change it announced.

words.meaning: A nickname, often a funny or affectionate one.
examples: The quiet goalkeeper earned the {sobriquet} ’the Wall’.
wrong: His sobriquet was the full legal name on his passport.

words.meaning: Something a person strongly hates or totally rejects.
examples: Waste of any kind is {anathema} to my grandmother.
wrong: Chocolate is anathema to him, so he eats it every day.

words.meaning: Something that causes constant trouble or misery.
examples: Slow internet is the {bane} of my working life.
wrong: The new tool was the bane of the team because it made work easier.

words.meaning: Something enormous and powerful, such as a huge company or object.
examples: The tiny startup took on a retail {behemoth}.
wrong: The behemoth was small enough to fit in her pocket.

words.meaning: A false story or rumor spread on purpose.
examples: The claim that the mayor had resigned was an old {canard}.
wrong: Everyone trusted the canard because it was completely true.

words.meaning: An idea or hope that is impossible to achieve.
examples: A world with no traffic is a {chimera} in this city.
wrong: The chimera came true the following morning.

words.meaning: A small, close group of people who share an interest and keep others out.
examples: She was surrounded by a {coterie} of loyal advisers.
wrong: The coterie welcomed anyone who wanted to join.

words.meaning: A lack of something, or too little of it.
examples: There is a {dearth} of affordable housing in the capital.
wrong: A dearth of volunteers meant we had far too many helpers.

words.meaning: A confused, embarrassing and complicated situation.
examples: The minister was caught up in a diplomatic {imbroglio}.
wrong: The imbroglio was simple, calm and easy to solve.

words.meaning: A huge force or group that crushes everything in its way.
examples: The champions were a {juggernaut} that nobody could stop.
wrong: The juggernaut lost every match by a wide margin.

words.meaning: A noisy fuss or argument, usually about something small.
examples: There was a {kerfuffle} over who had booked the room.
wrong: The kerfuffle was a long, quiet silence.

words.meaning: A situation of violent confusion and strong feeling.
examples: She was swept into a {maelstrom} of press attention.
wrong: The maelstrom was a calm and peaceful afternoon.

words.meaning: An unpleasant smell or an unhealthy, heavy atmosphere.
examples: A {miasma} of suspicion hung over the office.
wrong: The miasma filled the room with fresh, clean air.

words.meaning: A central point where several things connect.
examples: The station is the {nexus} of the city’s rail network.
wrong: The nexus was the most isolated, unconnected point on the map.

words.meaning: A complete, impressive range of something.
examples: The festival offers a {panoply} of music from every continent.
wrong: The panoply consisted of just one small item.

words.meaning: A perfect example of a quality.
examples: She was a {paragon} of patience with her students.
wrong: As a paragon of honesty, he lied whenever he could.

words.meaning: A very small amount of money, usually unfairly small.
examples: The workers were paid a {pittance} for long shifts.
wrong: She earned a pittance and became a millionaire in a month.

words.meaning: A very steep cliff, or a point close to disaster.
examples: The economy was on the {precipice} of collapse.
wrong: We stood on the precipice, safely in the middle of a flat field.

words.meaning: A difficult situation that is hard to get out of.
examples: The project sank into a legal {quagmire}.
wrong: The quagmire was quick and easy to escape.

words.meaning: A short break from something difficult or unpleasant.
examples: The rain brought a brief {respite} from the heat.
wrong: The respite made the hard work even more nonstop.

words.meaning: A split between groups caused by strong disagreement.
examples: The vote caused a deep {schism} within the party.
wrong: The schism brought every member into full agreement.

words.meaning: An object believed to bring good luck or protection.
examples: He carried the old coin as a {talisman} during exams.
wrong: She kept the talisman because she thought it brought bad luck.

words.meaning: A whirling mass of air or water, or a situation that pulls you in.
examples: The boat was caught in a {vortex} near the rocks.
wrong: The vortex was a perfectly still pond.

words.meaning: The money or means needed to do something.
examples: They lacked the {wherewithal} to rebuild after the flood.
wrong: Having the wherewithal, she couldn’t afford a single thing.

words.meaning: A very large, destructive fire.
examples: The {conflagration} destroyed half the old town.
wrong: The conflagration was a tiny candle flame.

words.meaning: Waste or broken pieces left after something.
examples: The beach was covered in the {detritus} of the storm.
wrong: The detritus was the newest, cleanest part of the house.

words.meaning: Floating wreckage, or useless odds and ends.
examples: Bits of {flotsam} washed up after the shipwreck.
wrong: The flotsam sank straight to the bottom of the sea.

words.meaning: The whole range of something.
examples: Her emotions ran the {gamut} from joy to despair.
wrong: The gamut covered only one single option.

words.meaning: The highest point of perfection or achievement.
examples: This novel is the {acme} of her writing.
wrong: His worst performance was the acme of his career.

words.meaning: Something that protects or defends against danger.
examples: A free press is a {bulwark} against corruption.
wrong: The bulwark left the town open to every attack.

words.meaning: A severe test or hard situation that creates something new.
examples: The war was the {crucible} in which the nation was formed.
wrong: The crucible was an easy time that changed nothing.
